title: What lies below the waterline of sustainable AI skills · hancrafted
description: When a task you keep explaining should become a skill, how to write its description as the moment you'd need it, what goes into the skill and what stays in project context, and what a shared skill needs to stay right: an owner, a version, tests and a retirement date.

What a skill is (2/5) Page 2 of 5 How AI discovers and reads a skill How AI discovers a skill, then reads it and its supporting files only when needed. The concept Progressive disclosure “Progressive disclosure defers advanced or rarely used features to a secondary screen, making applications easier to learn and less error-prone.” Nielsen Norman Group, Jakob Nielsen, Progressive Disclosure (nngroup.com) For skills, Anthropic's docs say Claude loads information in stages as needed. overview detail extras The example: a skill loads in three levels 1 Always loaded every skill's name and description: the skill index about 100 tokens a skill, paid on every turn every SKILL.md front matter name: collect-sediment-sample description: Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. about 100 tokens per skill, unless the skill is user-only 2 Loaded when the skill is used its main instructions once a task matches its description the SKILL.md body, on activation 1. Hold the robot two metres above the seabed. 2. … 6. Label the sample. 3 Loaded only if needed references, templates and scripts In Claude, a script runs and only its output enters the conversation one file, when a step asks for it references/species-guide.md assets/label-template.md scripts/arm-preset.py scripts run through bash; only output enters context 1 2 3 Collect sediment sample 1 Hold the robot 2 m up 2 Check the camera 3 … 6 the manual's index: every card's tab in view species guide label template arm preset In the story: The pilot reads the manual's index, then one card, then only the extras a step asks for. Codex and Gemini CLI load in stages too Codex and Gemini CLI: metadata first, body on use

What a skill is (3/5) Page 3 of 5 Skills are static and dynamic context What's always loaded is static; a skill loads on demand, so it is dynamic. Project brief Index Collect sediment sample camera feed manual's index standing orders pulled card frames sonar logs The context window, top to bottom System prompt hidden starting instructions system prompt, tool schemas Skills the manual's index name and description of every SKILL.md Memory files your standing orders and the project brief AGENTS.md (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code) Static always loaded, in every interaction Skill instructions the pulled card SKILL.md body Tool results camera frames file contents Tool results sonar readings Bash output Tool results sample logs MCP replies Free space Dynamic loaded on demand, as the task goes on In the story: Before the dive: your orders, the brief and the index. During it: the card and everything the robot sends up. A skill is dynamic whether you call it at the start or the AI picks it mid-task. Static has exceptions, so take the split as a rule of thumb. Called or picked, still dynamic: /collect-sediment-sample at the start of a message in Claude Code, or the agent picks the skill mid-task; either way its SKILL.md body enters the window on demand. Exceptions: .claude/rules/ files with paths load only when matching files open; Gemini CLI loads further GEMINI.md files just in time; a skill set to user-only invocation keeps even its name and description out.

Names differ by app: ChatGPT says apps; Gemini, Connected Apps. Google's Day 3 advice: keep AGENTS.md tight, with a short catalog of skills at the bottom; “The cleanest setups use both.”

What a skill is (5/5) Page 5 of 5 Two ways to call a skill You call a skill by name, or the AI picks it from its description. Called by name · you choose Picked from its description · the AI chooses “Collect sediment sample, please.” > /collect-sediment-sample Collect sediment sample collect-sediment-sample opened by name the task, no skill named “Get us a sample from the seabed.” Skill index · the manual's index description: × 3 skills Collect sediment sample collect-sediment-sample /SKILL.md Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. Measure water column measure-water-column /SKILL.md Use when measuring temperature and salt by depth. Run camera survey run-camera-survey /SKILL.md Use when mapping a new stretch of seabed. you the AI the AI Called by name You name the skill, and the AI opens that skill. No guessing. In chat apps, name the skill: Claude name it in your message ChatGPT @collect-sediment-sample Gemini app @collect-sediment-sample At the start of your message, by app: Claude Code /collect-sediment-sample Copilot CLI /collect-sediment-sample Codex $collect-sediment-sample (or pick it from /skills) Picked from its description You say nothing about the skill. The AI matches the task to each description; the name and description you wrote are its only clues. A poor description, and the skill stays unused, however good its instructions are. Task: “We're at the new site. Get us a sample from the seabed.” matches one description: line. collect-sediment-sample /SKILL.md description: Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. measure-water-column /SKILL.md description: Use when measuring temperature and salt by depth. run-camera-survey /SKILL.md description: Use when mapping a new stretch of seabed. 56% · never opened (Vercel, one Next.js docs skill) One vendor's eval, one documentation skill: an illustration, not a rule for all skills. Told explicitly to use it, the agent opened it in 95% or more. Not “skills in general”, as Google's Day 3 retells it. In the story: Ask for the card, or let the pilot find it in the index. “Slash command” is Claude Code and Copilot CLI wording; “by name” holds in every app. Gemini CLI adds a step: the agent asks to activate a skill, and you consent before it loads.

A skill is a folder of instructions What a skill is made of A skill is a folder with a required SKILL.md (a name and a description, then the instructions) and optional scripts/, references/ and assets/ folders 1 . ChatGPT describes the same three parts in its own words: a name and description, workflow steps and supporting materials 2 . Sources (2) Agent Skills, Specification ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io OpenAI Academy, Skills ( opens in a new tab ) academy.openai.com Names differ by app Claude, ChatGPT and Codex say “Skills”, GitHub Copilot says “agent skills”, and the Gemini app turns Gems into skills for personal accounts on 17 December 2026 1 . Whether the Gemini app's skills are SKILL.md folders is not stated in the pages read; it is verified for Gemini CLI only 2 . Sources (2) Google, About the transition from Gems to skills (Gemini Apps Help) ( opens in a new tab ) support.google.com Google, Agent Skills in Gemini CLI ( opens in a new tab ) raw.githubusercontent.com The description is the routing line Google's Day 3 whitepaper calls the description “your routing algorithm” 1 . This is Google's framing of how a skill is chosen, not a measurement of how often it routes correctly. Sources (1) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Anthropic's definition of a skill Anthropic defines skills as “folders that include instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude can load when needed” 1 . The Slide quotes the sentence as written; “Claude” in it is Anthropic's product, and the Agent Skills standard (note 1) publishes the same folder format for other agents. Sources (1) Anthropic, Introducing Agent Skills ( opens in a new tab ) claude.com

How AI discovers and reads a skill Three levels, stated by the standard The Agent Skills standard names metadata (name and description, about 100 tokens) loaded at startup for all skills, the SKILL.md body when the skill is activated, and files in scripts/, references/ or assets/ only when required 1 . Anthropic states the same three levels 2 . Google's Day 3 whitepaper states them too: “1. Metadata (name + description) is always in the agent's context. 2. SKILL.md body is loaded only when the skill triggers. 3. Bundled resources are loaded strictly as needed” 3 . That is Google's description of the design, not a test that it works. Sources (3) Agent Skills, Specification ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Anthropic, Agent Skills (Claude Platform docs) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Other apps load in stages too Codex lists name, description and file path first and reads the full instructions when it decides to use a skill 1 ; Gemini CLI documents metadata first, body on activation 2 . For apps whose pages were not read, the three-level claim is inferred from the shared format. Sources (2) OpenAI, Build skills (Codex docs) ( opens in a new tab ) learn.chatgpt.com Google, Agent Skills in Gemini CLI ( opens in a new tab ) raw.githubusercontent.com Scripts: documented for Claude only Claude runs scripts through bash and “only their output enters context” 1 . The other vendors' pages read say bundled scripts exist but do not say what that does to context, so keep this claim to Claude. Google's Day 3 whitepaper adds one line, that scripts “execute without ever polluting the token window” 2 ; treat it as Google's statement, not as documented behaviour in other apps. Sources (2) Anthropic, Agent Skills (Claude Platform docs) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com What the skill index costs Day 3 calls the metadata cost “tiny” but recurring: it is paid “on every turn” 1 . That is Google's claim; the size of the index comes from the standard's figure of about 100 tokens per skill in note 1, not from Day 3. Sources (1) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Progressive disclosure, as Anthropic names it Anthropic's docs say the filesystem-based design “allows progressive disclosure: Claude loads information in stages as needed, rather than consuming context upfront” 1 . The concept is general; a skill is the example. Sources (1) Anthropic, Agent Skills (Claude Platform docs) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Progressive disclosure, as Nielsen Norman Group defines it Jakob Nielsen's article defines it in its summary: “Progressive disclosure defers advanced or rarely used features to a secondary screen, making applications easier to learn and less error-prone” 1 . It is an interaction-design principle from 2006, older than skills; the Slide quotes it as written. Sources (1) Nielsen Norman Group, Jakob Nielsen, Progressive Disclosure ( opens in a new tab ) nngroup.com

Skills are static and dynamic context Static and dynamic, as Google defines them Static context is always loaded: system instructions, rule files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md), global memory and persona definitions; dynamic context is loaded on demand: skill instructions triggered by task matching, tool results, retrieved documents and windowed session history 1 . This is Google's vendor framing of the vendors' own mechanics, not a measured result. Sources (1) Osmani, Saboo and Kartakis, The New SDLC With Vibe Coding (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Why static and dynamic context are kept apart Day 1 says static context “is expensive because every token is present in every interaction, regardless of relevance”, and that too much of it “wastes tokens and dilutes signals” while too little “means the agent forgets critical rules” 1 . Day 3 repeats the split for the two files: “From one side AGENTS.md is always loaded within the project; Skills load on demand.” 2 Sources (2) Osmani, Saboo and Kartakis, The New SDLC With Vibe Coding (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Static instructions are a rule of thumb Instructions are not strictly static. Claude Code .claude/rules/ files with paths load only when matching files open 1 , Gemini CLI loads further GEMINI.md files just in time when a tool touches a directory 2 , and Copilot path-specific instructions apply by file match 3 . By default, a skill's name and description are always loaded too, unless the skill is set to user-only invocation 4 . Sources (4) Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project (Claude Code docs) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com Google, Provide context with GEMINI.md files (Gemini CLI docs) ( opens in a new tab ) raw.githubusercontent.com GitHub, Adding repository custom instructions for GitHub Copilot ( opens in a new tab ) docs.github.com Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code docs) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com

Instructions, skills and connectors Instructions are always loaded, skills are not Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md “at the start of every session” and loads a skill “on demand” 1 . Codex, Gemini CLI and GitHub Copilot document the same split for their instruction files and skills 2 . ChatGPT custom and project instructions were not read, and whether the Gemini app loads its instructions at the start of each session is unverified, so the split is not confirmed for those two apps. Sources (2) Anthropic, Extend Claude Code (Claude Code docs) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com GitHub, Adding agent skills for GitHub Copilot CLI ( opens in a new tab ) docs.github.com Names in chat apps Claude calls them Instructions, project instructions and Connectors 1 ; ChatGPT now says “apps (formerly connectors)” 2 ; the Gemini app says “Instructions for Gemini” and “Connected Apps” 3 . Sources (3) Anthropic, Understanding Claude's personalization features (Help Center) ( opens in a new tab ) support.claude.com OpenAI Academy, Skills ( opens in a new tab ) academy.openai.com Google, Manage your tasks and workflows in Gemini Apps (Help) ( opens in a new tab ) support.google.com Connectors reach, skills know how Connectors are Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that add tools and data, not guidance 1 . Anthropic describes MCP as the connection and a skill as the knowledge of how to use it 2 . Sources (2) GitHub, About Model Context Protocol (MCP) (Copilot docs) ( opens in a new tab ) docs.github.com Anthropic, Extend Claude Code (Claude Code docs) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com Skill vs. AGENTS.md, as Google puts it Day 3 has a “Skill vs. AGENTS.md” passage: “From one side AGENTS.md is always loaded within the project; Skills load on demand. The cleanest setups use both.” It advises keeping AGENTS.md tight and, if needed, using it as a router into the skills library “with a short catalog at the bottom that tells the agent what's available” 1 . Day 1 calls always-loaded rule files static context 2 . Both are Google's vendor guidance on how to split the two, not evidence that the split works. Sources (2) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Osmani, Saboo and Kartakis, The New SDLC With Vibe Coding (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com

Two ways to call a skill Calling a skill by name differs by app Claude Code runs /skill-name at the start of a message 1 ; Codex uses $ or /skills 2 ; ChatGPT and the Gemini app use @ 3 ; Copilot CLI uses a slash before the name 4 . Gemini's own help pages disagree on / versus @ for the Gemini app 5 6 , so the Slide shows @ and the note keeps /. “Slash command” is Claude Code and Copilot CLI wording; “by name” holds for all. Sources (6) Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code docs) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com OpenAI, Build skills (Codex docs) ( opens in a new tab ) learn.chatgpt.com OpenAI Academy, Skills ( opens in a new tab ) academy.openai.com GitHub, Adding agent skills for GitHub Copilot CLI ( opens in a new tab ) docs.github.com Google, Manage your tasks and workflows in Gemini Apps (Help) ( opens in a new tab ) support.google.com Google, About the transition from Gems to skills (Gemini Apps Help) ( opens in a new tab ) support.google.com The model picks a skill by its description Unless you name a skill, the model matches the task to the description. Gemini CLI adds a step: the model asks to activate a skill and the user consents before it is injected 1 . Sources (1) Google, Agent Skills in Gemini CLI ( opens in a new tab ) raw.githubusercontent.com Skills left unused: what the 56% measures “In 56% of eval cases, the skill was never invoked”: the documentation skill in Vercel's default configuration for Next.js 16 APIs, not all skills in general 1 . Explicit instructions to use it raised invocation to 95% or more, and the pass rate from 53% to 79% 1 . In the default configuration the skill tied the no-skill baseline overall at 53% 1 . One vendor's eval, no named model, no replication, so treat it as an illustration. Sources (1) Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals ( opens in a new tab ) vercel.com Unused skills in Google's Day 3: two misreadings of Vercel Google's Day 3 writes “a 56% non-invocation rate for skills expected to activate consistently” 1 . That turns one Next.js docs skill into skills in general, and calls Vercel's eval suite a “production analysis”. It also says “a skill stripped of its instructions scored 58%, while the agent without the skill scored 63%” 1 . In Vercel's post that is the default skill against the baseline on the test sub-score alone, not a stripped skill, and overall pass rates were equal at 53% 2 . Vercel's own wording wins. Day 3 is Google's vendor guidance on how to use skills, not evidence that skills go unused. Sources (2) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals ( opens in a new tab ) vercel.com

A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:31 You are the captain Imagine you work with an AI model that is brilliant at its job, the most capable colleague you have. I will give it a picture, because we need one all the way down: you are the captain of a coastal research project, and the model is your pilot of ten years, who steers a diving robot on a cable from the control room on deck while you decide where the project goes next. 0:31 – 0:53 One settled condition Your pilot has one condition, and it never changes. He forms no new memories overnight, but he keeps everything he ever learnt as a pilot, every rule of the trade. That is an AI model: what it learnt in training stays, and what you told it in yesterday's conversation is gone.

What a skill is 0:00 – 0:23 Surface first We are still at the surface, so before we ask when to write a skill, let's see what a skill is made of. I'll use the words your chat app uses, and if you work with a coding agent, some Slides have a second view that shows you the files behind each part. 0:23 – 0:39 The mechanics, plainly I want to be exact about how a skill gets loaded, because everything later depends on it. So I say first what the AI really does, and use the dive only to make it easier to picture.

A skill is a folder of instructions 0:00 – 0:37 Name and use-when A skill is a folder of instructions, and the company that introduced skills says so in almost those words. The folder holds one file it cannot do without, and that file starts with a name and a description, one line saying when to use it. That line matters more than it looks, because it is the first thing the model sees and, as you'll hear in a minute, often the only thing. On our card it is the title and the “use when” line in the head. 0:37 – 1:03 Steps in the body Then come the instructions, the procedure itself as numbered steps, in the body of the card. Beside that file a skill can carry optional supporting files that its steps reach for, like a species guide, a label template or an arm preset tucked into the card's sleeve. So a skill is a procedure, plus the material that procedure needs. 1:03 – 1:21 For developers If you work with a coding agent, switch to the coding-agent view, where the two parts of the file are called its frontmatter and the body of SKILL.md, and you can open and edit each. If you don't, you can ignore that view completely.

How AI discovers and reads a skill 0:00 – 0:29 The concept So how does the model find a skill, and how much of it does it read? Interface designers met the same problem long before AI: a screen that shows every option at once overwhelms the person using it, so you show the basics first and open the rest when someone needs it. They call it progressive disclosure, and a skill is loaded the same way, in three levels. 0:29 – 0:48 Step one Level one is how the model discovers a skill, and it is always loaded: every skill's name and description. So even with a hundred skills installed, all the model carries into every conversation is that short index, the index page of the manual. 0:48 – 1:03 Step two Level two is loaded when the skill is used. Only when a task matches a description does the model read that skill's main instructions, and not a moment before, the way the pilot pulls one card. 1:03 – 1:24 Step three Level three is loaded only if needed: the references, templates and scripts, the extras in the sleeve, which the model opens only when a step sends it there. The exact behaviour differs a little from app to app, so I keep the precise claims in the notes beside this Slide.

Skills are static and dynamic context 0:00 – 0:15 Back to the window Some of you have seen the context window Explorable, where we looked at everything the model holds in its head at once. This is the same context window, and now we place skills in it. 0:15 – 0:47 The standing part Start with what is there before any task begins, in the order the Explorable shows it: the system prompt, the skills, meaning the name and description of every skill, and the memory files, meaning your instructions in AGENTS.md. On our ship that is the standing rules, the manual's index, and your standing orders and the project brief. That part is static, so it sits in the window whatever the task turns out to be. 0:47 – 1:21 Filling as you dive Then the task begins and the window fills up: the skill the model opened, and the tool results it gets back, the camera frames, sonar readings and sample logs of the dive. That part is dynamic, and a skill's instructions belong to it, whether you call the skill at the start or the model picks it halfway through. So a skill sits on both sides of the line: its name and description are static, and the skill itself is dynamic.

Instructions, skills and connectors 0:00 – 0:21 Four things in the room Four things shape what the model knows, and they do four different jobs: personal instructions, project instructions, skills and connectors. In the control room they are your notebook, the project brief on the wall, the manual at the console, and the cable to the sonar and the lab database. 0:21 – 0:57 Read the tags Take them one at a time. Personal instructions are static, and they follow you into every project, as your notebook comes with you onto any ship. Project instructions are static too, but only inside this one project. Skills are dynamic, because one arrives when a task needs it, and a connector's results are dynamic too, because they arrive from another system while you work; the connector also lets the model act in that system. That is the split from the last Slide, now with names. 0:57 – 1:18 Your words may differ Your app may use other words for these four, so match the job, not the word. And if you work with a coding agent, the other view shows the files: your personal instructions file, AGENTS.md for the project, a SKILL.md for each skill, and a server for each connector.

Two ways to call a skill 0:00 – 0:17 By name There are two ways a skill gets used. The first is the simple one: you call it by name, the way you would tell the pilot “Collect sediment sample, please”, and the model opens that skill. No guessing involved. 0:17 – 0:39 By description In the second you say nothing about the skill. The model reads the descriptions while it works and decides for itself that this task needs one.
